unit.name: Food Science & Nutrition
unit.subtitle: Food commodities, macronutrients and micronutrients, planning balanced diets, the chemistry of cooking, and how heat and ingredients change food.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse the two categories or fail to give the spec definitions. Macronutrients are 'a class of chemical compounds which humans consume in the largest quantities' (protein, fats, carbohydrates). Micronutrients are 'required by humans throughout life in small quantities to facilitate a range of physiological functions' (vitamins, minerals, trace elements). The exact definitions are listed in the spec and routinely tested.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas C560QS specification, section 2 'Principles of nutrition'.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students label any cooking method as 'conduction' without identifying which heat-transfer mechanism applies. The spec is explicit that students must understand conduction, convection AND radiation, and that some dishes rely on more than one method (e.g. baking a potato uses conduction through the metal tray, convection of hot air in the oven, and radiation from the element). Naming all three and giving worked dish examples is high-tariff content.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas C560QS specification, section 4 'The science of food': 'how heat is transferred to food through conduction, convection and radiation and how and why the production of some dishes rely on more than one method of heat transference'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Functional properties — naming the right one
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students recall the term 'gelatinisation' without being able to apply it. The spec lists very specific functional terms — gelatinisation and dextrinization (carbohydrates); shortening, aeration, plasticity, emulsification (fats / oils); coagulation, foam formation, gluten formation, denaturation — physical, heat and acid (protein); enzymic browning and oxidisation (fruit / vegetables). These are vocabulary that must be matched precisely to the right ingredient and process.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas C560QS specification, section 4 'The science of food', 'working characteristics, functional and chemical properties of ingredients'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Food poisoning bacteria — naming all four
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students name only salmonella when the spec lists four food-poisoning organisms: salmonella, campylobacter, e-coli, staphylococcus. Each has distinct sources, signs and symptoms. A short-answer item asking to name two examples and their sources is foreseeable.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas C560QS specification, section 4 'The science of food', 'food spoilage' bullet on poisoning organisms.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat 'food security' and 'food poverty' as synonyms. The spec separates them: food poverty is the financial inability to afford a healthy diet at the household scale; food security is the broader principle of access to safe sufficient food for ALL (citing the World Health framing). Both terms appear in section 5 and need to be defined separately.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas C560QS specification, section 5 'Where food comes from': 'sustainability of food: the impact of food waste on the environment, local, global markets and communities, effect of food poverty' and 'food security: access to safe sufficient food for all (World Health)'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Cuisine has a precise spec definition
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe 'cuisine' as 'food from a country'. The spec gives a definition that examiners use in mark schemes: 'a style characteristic of a particular country or region, where the cuisine has developed historically using distinctive ingredients, specific preparation and cooking methods or equipment, and presentation or serving techniques.' Top-band answers cite all three pillars (ingredients, methods / equipment, presentation).
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas C560QS specification, section 5 'Where food comes from'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Sensory evaluation requires a panel and a method
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students write 'I asked some friends if they liked it' as sensory evaluation. The spec expects students to set up tasting panels for preference testing, use sensory descriptors correctly, and choose between sensory tests appropriately. Method, control, and descriptive vocabulary are all assessed.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas C560QS specification, section 6 'Cooking and food preparation': 'how to set up tasting panels for preference testing' and Appendix A skill 20 'Judge and manipulate sensory properties'.

common_misconceptions.topic: Adapting a recipe is more than swapping an ingredient
common_misconceptions.misconception: Students answer 'How would you adapt this recipe to be lower in saturated fat?' by replacing one ingredient. The spec expects students to consider ingredients AND processes AND cooking methods AND portion sizes together (e.g. replace butter with oil, change roasting to steaming, reduce portion size). Top-band answers change at least two of those four levers.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas C560QS specification, section 6 'Cooking and food preparation' under 'Developing recipes and meals': 'making decisions about the ingredients, processes, cooking methods, and portion sizes'.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat 'vegetarian' as one category. The spec names three: lacto-ovo (eats dairy and eggs), lacto (eats dairy, no eggs), vegan (no animal products at all). Each has different protein-complementation needs, different B12 considerations, different calcium sources. Conflating them loses application marks.
common_misconceptions.source: Eduqas C560QS specification, section 3 'Diet and good health': 'lifestyle needs to include vegetarians: lacto-ovo, lacto, vegan'.

student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Multiple Choice: Candidates leave items blank rather than committing to a best guess. Stimulus-based items reward a careful read of the stem (a food label, a recipe extract, a short scenario) before answering. Every mark counts on a 100-mark, 105-minute paper.
student_errors_by_question_type.1 mark — Identify / Name: Candidates write a sentence when one term is required. Use single nouns or named items where the question stem is 'Name' or 'Identify' — extra words add no marks and waste exam time.
student_errors_by_question_type.2 marks — State / Give: Candidates give one developed point when 2 marks usually requires either two distinct points or one point with development. Use the structure: point + qualifier (e.g. 'Vitamin A — needed for healthy vision').
student_errors_by_question_type.3 marks — Describe: Candidates state features without describing them. Aim for three distinct points or two with development. For named items (vitamins, minerals, food-poisoning bacteria) include function / symptom alongside the name.
student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Explain: Candidates list facts instead of giving reasons. Explain answers must use 'because', 'this means that' or 'as a result' to link cause and effect. Two reasons each with development typically reaches the top band.
student_errors_by_question_type.6 marks — Explain (Extended Response): Candidates give multiple short points without development. Aim for two or three well-developed reasons with food-science vocabulary, not six brief bullets.
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Discuss / Analyse (Extended Re: Candidates give one side of an argument and stop. 'Discuss' and 'Analyse' both require multiple perspectives weighed. Without considering more than one factor, candidates cap mid-band even when their facts are correct.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Evaluate (Extended Response): Candidates describe rather than evaluate. Top-band responses weigh advantages and disadvantages, reach a supported judgement, and apply named technical vocabulary (specific functional properties, named nutrients, named cooking methods). The judgement must be present — not implied.

topic_weighting_notes: The written paper is worth 50% of the qualification — 100 marks across 1 hour 45 minutes. The other 50% is the non-examination assessment (Food Investigation 15% + Food Preparation Assessment 35%). This build covers the written paper only because the NEA is project work, not lesson revision.

The written paper has two sections: stimulus-based questions and structured short / extended response questions. Both sections cover the six areas of content equally — there is no weighting that lets students drop a topic area.

Assessment objective weighting on the written paper: AO1 (Demonstrate knowledge and understanding) 20% and AO2 (Apply knowledge and understanding) 20% and AO4 (Analyse and evaluate) 10% — total 50%. AO3 (planning, preparing, cooking, presenting) is assessed entirely in the NEA. So the written paper rewards balanced recall + application + evaluation, with the heaviest skill being apply-not-just-recall.

Six areas of content sit equally on the spec but have different teaching density. Areas 2-3 (nutrition + diet / health) and area 4 (food science) are conceptually heaviest and consume more lessons in this build. Area 1 (commodities) is broad but shallow per item. Area 5 (provenance) and area 6 (cooking and food preparation) link practical skills to written-paper questions on food choice and recipe development.
Content is linear — all assessment in May / June each year. There is no early-entry or banking option.

Highest extended-response cap is 12 marks (Evaluate). Levels-based extended response questions appear at 6, 8 and 12 marks across the paper. Use StudyVault rubric (Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging) for all of these.
current_spec_changes: Specification (C560QS) is at version 2, last amended January 2019. The amendment was to the 'Making entries' section to clarify resit rules and carry-forward of NEA marks — no change to examinable subject content.
First teaching from 2016, first award from 2018. Linear qualification, summer assessment series only.

The qualification is not available for candidates in maintained schools and colleges in Wales — the WJEC equivalent (3550QS, called 'Food and Nutrition') serves Welsh centres. The two specifications share most content but have different titles and entry codes.
pedagogical_notes: EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning (effect size +8 months) — explicitly model how to turn a recall fact into an extended response. For Food Preparation and Nutrition this means walking through: 'I recall that gelatinisation is starch swelling in liquid above 60 degrees Celsius → I apply it to a sauce thickening as it heats → I link the method (whisking, even temperature) to the result (smooth, no lumps) → I justify why a roux gives more reliable thickening than a slurry'. Students do not chain reasoning automatically.

EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools — disciplinary literacy is critical. Students must use precise vocabulary (denaturation vs coagulation, gelatinisation vs dextrinization, food poverty vs food security, lacto vs lacto-ovo). Teach a 5-7 term glossary at the top of each lesson and drill it via flashcards — imprecise synonyms lose marks at every level.

Retrieval practice — the spec contains dense lists of named items (six commodity groups; nine essential amino acids; five-plus B vitamins; four food-poisoning bacteria; ten functional properties; three vegetarian categories; six-plus religious / lifestyle diets). Short, frequent low-stakes retrieval quizzes outperform single long revision sessions for this kind of named-list content. Each lesson ends with a 5-question knowledge check for this reason.

Dual coding supports recall of process and category content — heat transfer (conduction / convection / radiation), the danger zone, the bacterial growth curve, the carbohydrate hierarchy (mono → di → polysaccharide), and gelatinisation as a sequence. Pair every category list with a labelled diagram and a worded explanation; ask students to reproduce both halves from memory.

Worked examples for application questions — three sub-strands of the written paper are application-heavy: planning a balanced diet for a named individual, calculating energy and nutrients in a named recipe, and adapting a recipe to a brief. Model each one explicitly (highlight the brief, choose levers, justify) before students attempt the same template on a new scenario.

Concrete, real-food examples in every abstract concept. Functional properties, sensory descriptors, and culinary traditions all stick faster when tied to a named dish students could plausibly cook. Where the spec allows examples ('e.g.', 'such as'), use commodity-group dishes the student knows from their own NEA practical sessions.

Cause-and-effect chains feature heavily on this spec — e.g. saturated fat intake → raised LDL cholesterol → atherosclerosis → cardio-vascular disease. Treat these as worked-example lessons where the chain is built in front of students before they try one independently.

lessons_in_batch.title: Food Commodities & Their Place in the Diet
lessons_in_batch.description: The major commodity groups, the value of each in the diet, their characteristics, and why correct storage avoids contamination.
section_markers: bread cereals flour oats rice potatoes pasta

lessons_in_batch.title: Working Characteristics of Commodities
lessons_in_batch.description: How commodities behave when prepared and cooked — physical and chemical changes, complementary actions in recipes, and dry vs moist methods.
section_markers: prepare and cook dishes using commodities

lessons_in_batch.title: Macronutrients — Protein, Fats and Carbohydrates
lessons_in_batch.description: Definitions, functions and main sources of the three macronutrients — including essential amino acids, fat types, and the three carbohydrate groups.
section_markers: consequences of malnutrition over and under

lessons_in_batch.title: Micronutrients, Water and Dietary Fibre
lessons_in_batch.description: Fat-soluble and water-soluble vitamins, key minerals and trace elements, plus the dietary value of water and non-starch polysaccharides.
